Why Bother Auditing for AI?

Most businesses don't need a wholesale AI strategy. They need three or four specific problems solved. The audit process is how you find those problems — and, just as importantly, how you rule out the ones where AI would be a waste of time and money.

This guide walks you through a practical self-audit. No consultants required. No jargon. Just a structured way of looking at your own business and spotting where automation would actually help.

Be honest with yourself as you go through it. AI is genuinely useful in a fairly narrow set of circumstances. The goal here isn't to find uses for AI — it's to find the right uses, if any exist.

Step 1: Map Your Repetitive Processes

Start with the work that happens on repeat. Not the interesting, judgement-heavy work — the stuff that follows a pattern every time it runs.

Go through each department or function in your business and ask: what does this team do every week that looks roughly the same each time it's done?

Common examples include:

  • Screening and triaging inbound enquiries or requests
  • Pulling data from documents and entering it somewhere else
  • Generating quotes or proposals from a standard template
  • Responding to common customer questions
  • Compiling reports from multiple data sources
  • Monitoring websites, filings, or databases for changes
  • Categorising or tagging records, emails, or support tickets

Write these down without filtering them yet. The question at this stage is simply: what is repetitive?

What to look for

The strongest candidates for automation share a few characteristics. The task follows a consistent logic — even if the inputs vary, the process for handling them is largely the same. The task is time-consuming relative to its complexity. And the task doesn't require a relationship, a judgement call, or creative thinking to complete.

If a reasonably intelligent person could be trained to do the task from a written procedure, it's worth examining further.

Step 2: Estimate the Cost of Each Process

Now attach numbers to what you've listed. You don't need precision here — a rough estimate is enough to prioritise.

For each repetitive process, ask:

  • How many hours per week does this consume across everyone involved?
  • What is the rough hourly cost of the people doing it?
  • What is the error rate, and what does a mistake cost when it happens?
  • Does this process create a bottleneck that slows down other work?

Some processes will cost far more than they appear to. A task that takes two hours a week sounds minor, but if it's blocking a sales decision or delaying a client response, the real cost is much higher than the time alone.

Others will look expensive but turn out to be fast to complete manually and slow to automate correctly. Keep both possibilities in mind.

Step 3: Assess Your Data

AI systems need data to work with. Before you can automate a process, you need to understand what information flows through it — and whether that information exists in a usable form.

For each process on your list, ask:

  • What information does this process consume? (Emails, PDFs, spreadsheets, database records, web pages?)
  • Is that information structured (consistent fields, predictable format) or unstructured (free text, varied layouts)?
  • Where does it live? Is it accessible, or locked inside systems that don't expose it easily?
  • Is there enough historical data to train or test a system against?

Structured data — a spreadsheet of orders, a database of customer records — is generally easier to work with. Unstructured data — emails, PDFs, scanned documents — is harder but not impossible. Modern language models handle unstructured text surprisingly well, which is one of the more useful things they do.

A note on document-heavy businesses

If your business runs on documents — contracts, reports, applications, filings — there is often significant opportunity in automating how those documents are read, summarised, and acted on. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems can make your internal document library searchable and queryable in ways that manual searching simply cannot match. If your team spends real time hunting through files to answer questions, that's worth noting.

Step 4: Identify Decision Points

Not every step in a process needs to be automated. Often the most sensible approach is to automate the preparation work and keep a human in the loop for the actual decision.

Go back through your list and mark the decision points in each process. Ask:

  • Where does a human make a call that affects the outcome?
  • Is that call based on judgement, relationship, or policy?
  • Could the decision be made correctly from a well-structured summary of the relevant information?

If the answer to the last question is yes, the opportunity isn't necessarily to automate the decision — it's to automate everything that feeds into it. A system that reads an inbound request, pulls the relevant client history, checks stock or availability, and presents a one-page summary for a human to approve can save significant time even if the human still makes the final call.

This is an important point. Many businesses reject AI automation because they assume it means removing human oversight entirely. It doesn't have to. Configurable review gates — where the system does the groundwork and a human approves what matters — are often the most practical and trustworthy approach.

Step 5: Flag Privacy and Data Sensitivity

Before you go further, be honest about what data is involved in each process and what constraints apply to it.

Ask yourself:

  • Does this process handle personal data covered by UK GDPR?
  • Does it involve commercially sensitive information — pricing, contracts, client details?
  • Are there regulatory requirements around how this data is stored or processed?
  • Would sending this data to a third-party AI provider create a legal or reputational risk?

This isn't a reason to stop — it's a reason to be specific about what kind of system you'd need. Processes involving sensitive data often require private deployment: models running on your own infrastructure, or in-browser, with no data leaving your environment. That's entirely achievable, but it changes the implementation approach and cost.

Don't assume that because a process handles sensitive data it can't be automated. Assume instead that the automation needs to be designed with data control built in from the start.

Step 6: Score and Prioritise

By now you should have a list of candidate processes with some rough information attached to each. Score them against these four criteria:

  1. Volume: How often does this process run? Daily beats weekly beats monthly.
  2. Cost: What is the realistic time and error cost of doing this manually?
  3. Automability: How well-defined is the logic? How accessible is the data? How much does it vary?
  4. Risk: What happens if the automated system makes a mistake? Low-stakes errors are acceptable; high-stakes ones need human review gates.

Score each criterion on a simple scale — high, medium, low is enough. The processes that score high on volume and cost, medium-to-high on automability, and low-to-medium on risk are your starting points.

Don't try to automate everything at once. One well-built system that works reliably is worth more than five half-finished projects that require constant babysitting.

Step 7: Be Honest About What AI Cannot Do

This step is the one most AI vendors skip. It's also the one that will save you the most money.
